pos: a. (of a strong or obstinate heart; in the Authorized Version, stubborn against God rather than courageous)
etymology: From stout, Old French estout, bold, proud, and heart. English has since made stout-hearted a compliment; the Authorized Version uses it only of men whose strength is set against the LORD.
biblical_def: Modern English hears stouthearted and thinks of courage. Scripture uses it twice, and both times it means obstinate. The first is a picture of a battlefield the morning after God has acted: “The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands” (Psa 76:5). The strong men are asleep — a psalmist's way of saying dead — and their hands, the hands that held the weapons, cannot be found by them. Stoutness of heart availed nothing. The second is a summons to a class of people, and it defines the term: “Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness” (Isa 46:12). The stouthearted are identified precisely as those far from righteousness — not far because they are weak, but far because they are strong in themselves. And the answer given them is the gospel in miniature: “I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry” (Isa 46:13). They are far from righteousness, so God brings the righteousness near. That is exactly the exchange Paul describes of his own countrymen, “going about to establish their own righteousness” and not submitting to God's (Rom 10:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stouthearted as having a brave heart; and stout as bold, intrepid, but also obstinate, resolute in a bad sense, proud.
webster_full: STOUT, a. [Old Fr. estout, bold, proud.]
1. Strong; lusty; vigorous; robust; sinewy; muscular.
2. Bold; intrepid; valiant; brave.
3. Obstinate; resolute; proud; as a stout heart.
STOUTHE'ARTED, a. Having a brave heart; but in Scripture used of the obstinate. Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness. Is. 46.
scriptures: Isaiah 46:12
Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness:
Psalm 76:5
The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands.
Isaiah 46:13
I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry: and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory.
Romans 10:3
For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: The age has made stoutness of heart the chief virtue — resilience, self-belief, never backing down — which is the exact condition Isaiah addresses as distance from righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Every popular philosophy of the moment counsels a stout heart: believe in yourself, never quit, be unbreakable. The counsel is not worthless in its place — Scripture commends courage and rebukes cowardice. But Isaiah 46:12 identifies a strength that is itself the barrier: men far from righteousness precisely because nothing has ever broken them. The Reformed doctrine of conviction of sin exists because a heart that has never been made soft cannot receive a righteousness it did not earn. Psalm 76:5 is the end of that road, and the detail is terrible — the men of might could not find their own hands.

The churchly form is self-righteousness, and Paul names it in his own people with grief rather than contempt: they were going about to establish their own righteousness, and the phrase describes enormous religious effort. The stouthearted man in a pew is not lazy; he is working very hard on a project God has already declared bankrupt. Isaiah 46:13 is the only remedy offered anywhere in Scripture, and it does not ask the stouthearted to travel: I bring near my righteousness. He closes the distance Himself, and the one thing required of the strong man is that he stop manufacturing a rival.
roots_summary: Hebrew abbire leb (H47, H3820), the mighty of heart, the stubborn-hearted; tsedaqah (H6666), righteousness; abbir, a bull or strong one.
roots_lines: Hebrew abbire leb (H47, H3820) — mighty ones of heart; Isaiah 46:12, with abbir also used of bulls and stallions.
Hebrew abbire leb at Psalm 76:5 — the same phrase, there rendered stouthearted and applied to slain warriors.
Hebrew rechoqim mitstsedaqah (H7350, H6666) — far from righteousness; the diagnosis attached to the title.
Hebrew qerabti tsidqathi (H7126) — I have brought near my righteousness; Isaiah 46:13, God closing the distance.
Old French estout — bold, proud; Webster's root, carrying both the courage and the obstinacy.
usage: “Ye stouthearted, that are far from righteousness” — the strength is the distance.
“None of the men of might have found their hands” — the end of that road.
“I bring near my righteousness” — He closes the distance Himself.

pos: pp. (scorned; thought unworthy of notice or regard)
etymology: Old French desdaignier, from Latin dedignari, to think unworthy, from de- and dignus, worthy. To disdain is to judge a man beneath consideration — a verdict on his worth, not merely a dislike.
biblical_def: Both occurrences show a strong man assessing a weak one and getting the verdict badly wrong. The first is in the valley of Elah: “And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance” (1Sa 17:42). Goliath's estimate was entirely accurate as far as it went — David was a youth, and unarmoured. What the giant could not see was the variable David named a moment later: “I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied” (1Sa 17:45). Disdain fails because it measures what is visible. The second occurrence is Job's, and it is harder to read charitably: “But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock” (Job 30:1). Job, in his misery, admits that he would once have thought these men's fathers beneath his sheepdogs — and now their sons mock him. Scripture records the sentence without softening it, and the reader is left to notice that the man who once disdained is now disdained.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disdain as to think unworthy; to deem worthless; to consider to be unworthy of notice, care, or regard; to scorn; and notes it implies a comparison of worth.
webster_full: DISDA'IN, v.t. [Fr. dedaigner; L. dedignor; de and dignor, to deem worthy.]
To think unworthy; to deem worthless; to consider to be unworthy of notice, care, regard, esteem, or unworthy of one's character.
Whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock. Job 30.
DISDA'IN, n. Contempt; scorn; a passion excited by the meanness or worthlessness of an object.
He disdained him: for he was but a youth. 1 Sam. 17.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:42
And when the Philistine looked about, and saw David, he disdained him: for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and of a fair countenance.
1 Samuel 17:45

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.
Job 30:1
But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock.
1 Corinthians 1:27
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: Contempt has become a public style, and a church that adopts it forfeits the one posture in which God is said to work.
corruption_paragraphs: Disdain is now a manner of speech rather than an occasional sin. Whole commentaries, feeds, and ministries operate in it, because contempt is engaging and because dismissing an opponent is quicker than answering him. 1 Corinthians 1:27 is the standing warning against making it a habit: God has chosen the foolish things to confound the wise and the weak things to confound the mighty, which means the person most easily disdained is statistically likely to be the instrument. Goliath's error was not stupidity. He read the evidence correctly and drew the wrong conclusion because the decisive factor was invisible to him.

Job 30:1 deserves to be read by anyone who has ever been on the receiving end. Job is the righteous sufferer of the book, vindicated by God at the end, and even he had held some men's fathers beneath his dogs. Scripture does not tidy this up. The honest reading is that disdain is a sin the godly commit too, usually about class, and usually without noticing — and that Job is now hearing from the sons what he once thought of the fathers. James 2 is the New Testament application: the man in the poor raiment and the man with the gold ring are assessed by the same congregation, and the assessment is called being judges of evil thoughts.
roots_summary: Hebrew bazah (H959), to despise, hold in contempt; ma'as (H3988), to reject as worthless; Latin dedignari, to think unworthy.
roots_lines: Hebrew wayyibzehu (H959) — and he despised him; 1 Samuel 17:42, the same verb used of Esau despising his birthright.
Hebrew ma'as (H3988) — to reject, refuse as worthless; Job 30:1, of the fathers Job would not have set with his dogs.
Hebrew sechoq (H7814) — laughter, derision; what Job now receives from their sons.
Hebrew YHWH tseba'oth (H6635) — the LORD of hosts, of armies; the invisible factor Goliath omitted from his calculation.
Latin de- and dignus — to judge unworthy; Webster's root, a verdict on worth.
usage: “He disdained him: for he was but a youth” — an accurate observation, a fatal conclusion.
“I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts” — the factor not on the giant's list.
“Whose fathers I would have disdained” — said by the righteous man of the book.

pos: pp. (quieted; pacified; calmed, as anger or a tumult)
etymology: Old French apaisier, to bring to peace, from a- and pais, peace, from Latin pax. To appease is to bring a thing to peace — and the Bible's two instances are both human, political, and hollow.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are of human anger or human crowds being quieted by circumstance rather than satisfied by justice. The first is the Persian court: “After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her” (Est 2:1). The king's rage burned itself out, and what followed was regret — but the decree stood, because a Persian decree could not be revoked. Anger cooled, and the damage remained. The second is the riot at Ephesus: “And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana” (Act 19:35). A civic official calms a mob with a speech about legal channels and the risk of being called to account — competent, prudent, and entirely without repentance in it. The idolatry that started the riot is untouched and is in fact affirmed by the man restoring order. Scripture reserves a different word for the quieting of God's wrath: not appeasement, which cools, but propitiation, which satisfies (Rom 3:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appease as to make quiet; to calm; to reduce to a state of peace; to still; to pacify; and to allay, as anger or tumult.
webster_full: APPE'ASE, v.t. s as z. [Fr. apaiser, from paix, peace; L. pax.]
1. To quiet; to calm; to still; to pacify; to reduce to a state of peace; to allay, as anger or excitement.
2. To still; to quiet, as tumult or agitation; to compose, as a storm.
APPE'ASED, pp. Quieted; calmed; stilled; pacified.
When the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased. Esther 2.
scriptures: Esther 2:1
After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her.
Acts 19:35

And when the townclerk had appeased the people, he said, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there that knoweth not how that the city of the Ephesians is a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?
Romans 3:25
Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
Proverbs 15:18
A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife.
corruption_summary: Appeasement is mistaken for peacemaking, in the world and in the church, and the quieting of a disturbance is counted as the settling of a wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 19:35 is a study in the difference between order and righteousness. The townclerk does an excellent job: he calms a dangerous mob, protects Paul's companions, and invokes the lawful assembly — and he does it by reassuring everyone that Diana is beyond dispute. Peace was restored and nothing was healed. Churches do this constantly. A conflict is managed, a complaint is absorbed, a difficult man is quieted, and the underlying wrong is left exactly where it was, because appeasement is faster than discipline and looks more like love. Proverbs 15:18 does commend the man who appeaseth strife — but the contrast there is with the wrathful man who stirs it, not with the man who addresses it.

The deeper reason the church must keep these words distinct is Christological. Rome's Mass, the treasury of merit, indulgences, and purgatory all operate on an appeasement model — anger gradually cooled by accumulated satisfactions. Romans 3:25 uses propitiation: God set forth His own Son, in His blood, to declare His righteousness. Divine wrath was not soothed; it was borne and exhausted. Esther 2:1 shows what mere appeasement leaves behind — a cooled king, a remembered grievance, and an irrevocable decree still standing. The cross leaves no decree standing against those who are in Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew shakak (H7918), to subside, abate; Greek katastello (G2687), to quiet, restrain; Greek hilasterion (G2435), propitiation; Latin pax, peace.
roots_lines: Hebrew keshok chamath hammelek (H7918) — when the king's heat subsided; Esther 2:1, the anger abating of itself.
Greek katasteilas (G2687) — having quieted, restrained; Acts 19:35, the townclerk settling the crowd.
Greek hilasterion (G2435) — propitiation, mercy seat; Romans 3:25, wrath satisfied rather than cooled.
Hebrew yashqit rib (H8252) — quieteth strife; Proverbs 15:18, the good sense of the word.
Latin pax, Old French apaisier — to bring to peace; Webster's root.
usage: “When the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased” — and the decree still stood.
“When the townclerk had appeased the people” — order restored, idolatry affirmed.
“A propitiation through faith in his blood” — not cooled; borne.

pos: pp. (made peaceful; appeased; the wrath being satisfied or quieted)
etymology: Latin pacificare, from pax, peace, and facere, to make — literally peace-made. The Authorized Version uses it once of a king and once of God, and the difference between those two is the gospel.
biblical_def: Set the two occurrences side by side. Of a man: “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified” (Est 7:10). Ahasuerus is pacified by an execution — the guilty man dies on his own gallows, and the king's anger is satisfied by a punishment that fell where it belonged. Of God: “That thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD” (Eze 16:63). This comes at the end of the most graphic chapter in the prophets, an unsparing account of Jerusalem's spiritual adultery — and it ends with God pacified. Notice what the pacification produces in the forgiven party: not celebration but silence. Never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame. The mouth that is stopped is the mouth of self-defence. Forgiveness in Scripture does not restore a sinner's case; it ends it. And the ground on which God can be pacified without ceasing to be just is named in the New Testament: a propitiation in the blood of Christ, that He might be just and the justifier (Rom 3:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pacify as to appease, as wrath or excitement; to calm; to still; to quiet; to allay agitation or passion; and to restore peace to.
webster_full: PAC'IFY, v.t. [L. pacifico; pax, peace, and facio, to make.]
1. To appease, as wrath or other violent passion or appetite; to calm; to still; to quiet; to allay agitation or excitement.
Then was the king's wrath pacified. Esther 7.
2. To restore peace to; to tranquilize; as, to pacify a country.
PAC'IFIED, pp. Appeased; tranquilized.
scriptures: Ezekiel 16:63
That thou mayest remember, and be confounded, and never open thy mouth any more because of thy shame, when I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD.
Esther 7:10
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.
Romans 3:25
Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
Romans 3:19
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
corruption_summary: A God who must be pacified is dismissed as primitive, and with Him goes the only account of forgiveness in which justice is not simply waived.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection is now standard: a God who needs to be pacified is a God of pagan temper, and the Christian God should simply forgive. The answer is in the two verses themselves. Esther 7:10 shows what pacification by execution looks like when the guilty party bears it — Haman on his own gallows, and nobody calls it primitive. Ezekiel 16:63 shows God pacified toward a people whose sins the chapter has just catalogued in unbearable detail. If He is pacified without any satisfaction at all, then the catalogue meant nothing and God is indifferent to what He spent a chapter describing. Romans 3:25 gives the only answer that keeps both: He is just, and the justifier, because the satisfaction fell on His own Son.

Ezekiel adds the pastoral note most likely to be missed. Being pacified toward a sinner produces in that sinner shame and a stopped mouth — never open thy mouth any more. Romans 3:19 uses the same figure of the whole world under the law: that every mouth may be stopped. Modern forgiveness aims at restoring the offender's self-regard; biblical forgiveness ends his argument. And it is precisely because the case is closed that the forgiven man is free. He is not carrying a defence any more, because Another has answered for him, and there is nothing left to say.
roots_summary: Hebrew kaphar (H3722), to cover, to make atonement, to pacify; shakak (H7918), to subside; Latin pacificare, to make peace.
roots_lines: Hebrew bekhapperi lakh (H3722) — when I make atonement for thee; Ezekiel 16:63, the great atonement verb rendered pacified.
Hebrew kaphar (H3722) — to cover, to ransom, to purge; the root of kapporeth, the mercy seat.
Hebrew shakakah (H7918) — subsided, abated; Esther 7:10, the king's heat going down after the hanging.
Greek hilasterion (G2435) — propitiation, the mercy seat; Romans 3:25, the Septuagint's word for kapporeth.
Latin pax and facere — peace made; Webster's root, and an exact description of the atonement.
usage: “Then was the king's wrath pacified” — by an execution, and on the guilty man's own gallows.
“When I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done” — the atonement verb, spoken by God.
“Never open thy mouth any more” — forgiveness ends the case; it does not reopen it.

pos: pp. (caught up with; come upon suddenly; and of sin, surprised into a fault)
etymology: From over and take. The picture is of something faster catching a man from behind — a pursuer, a storm, or a temptation that arrives before he has seen it coming.
biblical_def: The word appears twice and describes two kinds of pursuit. David of his enemies: “I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed” (Psa 18:37) — the deliberate, successful chase of a warrior king. Paul of a brother: “Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). This is one of the most carefully worded sentences in the New Testament and every clause is load-bearing. The man is overtaken — caught, surprised, not a settled rebel. The ones who act are ye which are spiritual, not the offended or the eager. The verb is restore, a word used of setting a broken bone and of mending nets. The manner is the spirit of meekness. And the safeguard is self-directed: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Then the next verse names the whole operation: “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2). Restoration is not leniency; it is the setting of a bone, which hurts and is meant to heal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overtake as to come up with in a course, pursuit or motion; to catch; and to come upon; to take by surprise.
webster_full: OVERTA'KE, v.t.
1. To come up with in a course, pursuit, progress or motion; to catch.
He pursued his enemies and overtook them.
2. To come upon; to fall on afterwards.
3. To take by surprise. If a man be overtaken in a fault, ye who are spiritual, restore such an one. Gal. 6.
scriptures: Galatians 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Psalm 18:37
I have pursued mine enemies, and overtaken them: neither did I turn again till they were consumed.
1 Corinthians 10:13

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
corruption_summary: Galatians 6:1 is either ignored, so that the fallen are discarded, or amputated at the word restore, so that no fault is ever named.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest failure is simple abandonment. A believer is overtaken, the matter becomes known, and the congregation's instinct is distance — not from doctrine but from embarrassment. Galatians 6:1 gives a command with an assigned party: ye which are spiritual. That is not a compliment to the willing; it is a qualification, and it means the work belongs to mature men who can be trusted with a broken bone. Where nobody accepts the assignment, the fallen man is left to set the fracture himself, which is why so many never walk right again.

The opposite error takes the word restore and drops everything around it, producing a ministry in which nothing is ever named as a fault and restoration means a swift return to public standing. Paul's sentence does not permit that either. It calls the thing a fault, it requires the spirit of meekness rather than warmth, and it attaches a warning to the restorer: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. The whole procedure assumes the man doing the mending is capable of the same fall, which is exactly what 1 Corinthians 10:13 says of every temptation — it is common to man. There are no specialists in immunity, only brothers with bone-setting work to do.
roots_summary: Greek prolambano (G4301), to take beforehand, to surprise; katartizo (G2675), to mend, set a bone, restore; prautes (G4240), meekness.
roots_lines: Greek prolemphthe (G4301) — be caught beforehand, surprised; Galatians 6:1, the man overtaken rather than settled in sin.
Greek katartizete (G2675) — mend, repair, set in joint; the word used of mending nets in Matthew 4:21.
Greek en pneumati prautetos (G4240) — in a spirit of meekness; the required manner, not an optional tone.
Greek skopon seauton (G4648) — watching yourself; the restorer's own guard, in the singular amid plurals.
Greek anthropinos (G442) — such as belongs to man; 1 Corinthians 10:13, no temptation is exotic.
usage: “If a man be overtaken in a fault” — caught from behind, not entrenched.
“Restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” — the word is used of setting a bone.
“Considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” — no specialists in immunity.

pos: n. pl. (those who rove without a settled home; in Hosea, a people scattered under judgment)
etymology: From wander, Saxon wandrian, to rove, connected with wend and wind — to go by a turning, uncertain course. The word carries aimlessness in its root, not merely travel.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are judgments, and they run in opposite directions. Jeremiah, against Moab: “Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles” (Jer 48:12). Moab had been settled on his lees, undisturbed from youth, never poured from vessel to vessel — and God sends wanderers to make him wander. The second is against Israel herself, and it is the severer of the two: “My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations” (Hos 9:17). The cause is named exactly: they did not hearken. Wandering in Scripture is the standing penalty for a people who would not stay put under God's word, and the sentence goes back to Cain — “a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth” (Gen 4:12). But the Bible also has a wandering that is not a curse at all, and Hebrews is careful to distinguish it: the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — men without a settled country because they were looking for a better one. The difference is not the walking; it is whether a man is driven from a home or heading toward one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wanderer as one who roves; a rambler; one that deviates from duty; and wander as to rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object.
webster_full: WAN'DERER, n. One that wanders; a rambler; one that roves; one that deviates from duty.
WAN'DER, v.i. [Sax. wandrian; from the root of wend, to go.]
1. To rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object in view.
2. To leave home; to depart; to migrate.
3. To depart from the subject in discussion. They shall be wanderers among the nations. Hos. 9.
scriptures: Hosea 9:17
My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations.
Jeremiah 48:12
Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will send unto him wanderers, that shall cause him to wander, and shall empty his vessels, and break their bottles.
Genesis 4:12
When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
Hebrews 11:13

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Rootlessness is now marketed as freedom, and the church has adopted the same restlessness under the name of following a call.
corruption_paragraphs: The culture has made a virtue of having no fixed place — the untethered life, the perpetual search, the refusal to settle — and Scripture consistently treats that condition as a judgment. Cain's sentence was to be a fugitive and a vagabond; Israel's was to be wanderers among the nations; and Moab's was to be poured from vessel to vessel after generations of comfortable stagnation. God does use dislocation to break settled complacency, as Jeremiah 48 shows. But wandering itself is never the goal, and a man who cannot stay anywhere has not achieved freedom.

The churchly version is transience dressed as guidance. Congregations are joined and left on preference, membership is treated as optional, and a believer may pass twenty years without ever being known well enough to be corrected. Hosea names the root cause of Israel's wandering, and it is not wanderlust: because they did not hearken unto him. Hebrews 11:13 keeps the one legitimate homelessness clearly marked — the patriarchs were strangers and pilgrims because they were persuaded of a promise and heading for a city. That is pilgrimage, which has a destination and usually a great deal of ordinary faithfulness in one place along the way. It is the opposite of drift.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadad (H5074), to flee, wander; na wanad (H5128, H5110), fugitive and vagabond; Greek parepidemos (G3927), a resident foreigner, pilgrim.
roots_lines: Hebrew nodedim (H5074) — wanderers, fugitives; Hosea 9:17, of Israel among the nations.
Hebrew tso'im (H6808) — tilters, those who tip vessels; Jeremiah 48:12, the wanderers sent to pour Moab out.
Hebrew na wanad (H5128, H5110) — tottering and wandering; Genesis 4:12, Cain's sentence, and the root of the land of Nod.
Greek xenoi kai parepidemoi (G3581, G3927) — strangers and pilgrims; Hebrews 11:13, homelessness with a destination.
Saxon wandrian — to rove by a turning course; Webster's root, aimlessness built in.
usage: “They shall be wanderers among the nations” — and the cause is they did not hearken.
“Wanderers, that shall cause him to wander” — Moab poured from vessel to vessel.
“Strangers and pilgrims on the earth” — the one homelessness that is not a curse.

pos: a. (last; in the rear; furthest behind)
etymology: From hinder, Saxon hinder, backward, with the superlative ending. The Authorized Version uses the older form; modern printings usually read hindmost.
biblical_def: Two occurrences, and in each one the rearmost place tells you what somebody loved. The first is Jacob's arrangement on the morning he expected to meet Esau and possibly die: “And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost” (Gen 33:2). The order is a confession. Jacob's favourites are furthest from the danger, and Leah — the wife he never chose — stands between Rachel and the sword with her six sons. Scripture records the arrangement without a word of comment and lets the reader draw the conclusion about a house ordered by preference. The second is Babylon's sentence: “Your mother shall be sore confounded; she that bare you shall be ashamed: behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert” (Jer 50:12). The empire that had been foremost among the nations is to become the hindermost, and the land that fed the world becomes desert. The Lord states the principle that governs both texts: “So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hindermost or hindmost as the last; that is behind all the others; and hinder as that is in a position behind another, opposed to fore.
webster_full: HIND'ERMOST, a. superl. [from hind.] The last; that is behind all others.
HIND'MOST, a. The last; that comes or is in the rear of all others.
Rachel and Joseph hindermost. Gen. 33.
HIND'ER, a. That is in a position behind another; opposed to fore; as the hinder part of a wagon.
From Sax. hinder, backward, behind.
scriptures: Genesis 33:2
And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost.
Jeremiah 50:12
Your mother shall be sore confounded; she that bare you shall be ashamed: behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.
Matthew 20:16
So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
Genesis 29:31
And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the order a man puts his household in reveals what he actually values.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is archaic and uncontested. What Genesis 33:2 holds is a quiet and devastating doctrine about households. Jacob had four women and eleven children, and when he thought death was coming up the road he ranked them. The handmaids and their sons went first, Leah and her six after, and Rachel and Joseph last where the danger would reach them latest. He did not announce a preference; he arranged a caravan, and the arrangement said everything. Fathers still do this, not with marching order but with attention, money, patience, and time.

The principle to recover is that God notices the hindermost and He notices the foremost, and He is not bound by either ranking. Genesis 29:31 records His response to Jacob's scale: when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb — and from that unloved wife came Judah, and from Judah came Christ. Jeremiah 50:12 shows the same reversal at the scale of empires, with the foremost of the nations becoming a desert. Matthew 20:16 states it as a law of the kingdom. Any man arranging his household by preference should reckon with the fact that the line of the Messiah ran through the wife who was placed in the middle of the column.
roots_summary: Hebrew acharonim (H314), the last, hindmost; acharith (H319), the latter end; Saxon hinder, backward.
roots_lines: Hebrew acharonim (H314) — the last, those behind; Genesis 33:2, of Rachel and Joseph in the rear.
Hebrew acharith goyim (H319, H1471) — the last of the nations; Jeremiah 50:12, of Babylon brought to the rear.
Hebrew senu'ah (H8130) — hated, the lesser-loved; Genesis 29:31, the Hebrew idiom for Leah's standing.
Greek hoi eschatoi protoi (G2078, G4413) — the last first; Matthew 20:16, the kingdom's reversal.
Saxon hinder — backward, behind; Webster's root, with the old superlative preserved in the Authorized Version.
usage: “Rachel and Joseph hindermost” — the caravan order was the confession.
“The hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness” — the foremost empire, brought to the rear.
“When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb” — and Judah was born.

pos: v.i. (to stagger; to incline in walking, first to one side then the other, as a drunken man)
etymology: Saxon hreol, a reel or winding frame; hence the verb, to whirl or stagger. Both Scripture uses pair it with the figure of a drunkard.
biblical_def: Both occurrences pair the word with drunkenness, and both describe a loss of footing that is not the walker's fault alone. The first is the great storm passage of Psalm 107: mariners caught in a tempest “reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end” (Psa 107:27). The Hebrew behind wits' end says literally that all their wisdom was swallowed up — competent seamen with nothing left to try. The next verse is the turn: “Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses” (Psa 107:28). The crying comes at the end of the resources, and the psalm treats that as the normal order rather than a failure. The second occurrence is cosmic: “The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again” (Isa 24:20). The planet itself staggers under the weight of its own transgression. Paul uses the same instability of Christians who have no doctrinal footing: “tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reel as to stagger; to incline or move in walking, first to one side and then to the other; to vacillate; and notes it of a drunken man or of one who is dizzy.
webster_full: REEL, v.i.
To stagger; to incline or move in walking, first to one side and then to the other; to vacillate.
He reels with weariness or drunkenness.
They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man. Ps. 107.
REEL, n. [Sax. hreol.] A frame or machine turning on an axis, on which yarn is extended for winding.
scriptures: Psalm 107:27
They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end.
Isaiah 24:20
The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.
Psalm 107:28
Then they cry unto the LORD in their trouble, and he bringeth them out of their distresses.
Ephesians 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
corruption_summary: Doctrinal instability is now described as openness, and a church with no footing is praised for being teachable.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 4:14 describes a congregation reeling — tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine — and Paul treats it as childishness to be outgrown, not humility to be admired. The contemporary translation of the condition is generous: such a church is exploratory, non-dogmatic, willing to hold things loosely. Paul names the mechanism instead: the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive. Somebody is steering. A body that will move with any wind is not free; it is available, and the apostle assumes someone is waiting to take it. The remedy he gives in the same passage is not less teaching but more — pastors and teachers, until the whole body comes to the unity of the faith.

Psalm 107:27 puts the other kind of reeling in a far kinder light. These are sailors in a real storm, and they reel because the sea is doing it to them; the psalm does not scold them for having exhausted their seamanship. It simply notes that at their wits' end they cried, and He brought them out. That is the pattern for every believer whose footing is gone through affliction rather than through drift. Isaiah 24:20 then sets the whole creation staggering under the weight of transgression, and even there the chapter ends with the LORD of hosts reigning in Zion. The earth reels; the throne does not.
roots_summary: Hebrew chagag (H2287), to reel, to move in a circle; nua (H5128), to totter, wander; chokmatham tithballa, their wisdom is swallowed up.
roots_lines: Hebrew yachoggu (H2287) — they reel, go round; Psalm 107:27, from a root also meaning to keep a festival by circling.
Hebrew nua tanua (H5128) — reeling it shall reel; Isaiah 24:20, the doubled verb of the staggering earth.
Hebrew kol chokmatham tithballa (H2451, H1104) — all their wisdom is swallowed up; the literal of at their wits' end.
Greek kludonizomenoi (G2831) — tossed by waves; Ephesians 4:14, the same instability applied to doctrine.
Saxon hreol — a winding frame; Webster's root, whence the whirling sense of the verb.
usage: “Reel to and fro… and are at their wits' end” — all their wisdom swallowed up.
“Then they cry unto the LORD” — at the end of the resources, and the psalm expects it.
“Carried about with every wind of doctrine” — and somebody is working the wind.

etymology: From over and past. Both occurrences describe a season of danger that has a term — something the believer waits out rather than escapes.
biblical_def: Twice the Authorized Version uses this word, and both times it is attached to a shelter and a stated limit. David, hiding in a cave from Saul: “Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast” (Psa 57:1). Note that the calamities are not removed; they are outlasted, under wings, in a cave. Isaiah gives the same counsel to a whole people on the eve of judgment: “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast” (Isa 26:20). The tenderness of the summons is remarkable — come, my people… shut thy doors — and it is issued immediately before the verse that says the LORD comes out of His place to punish the inhabitants of the earth (Isa 26:21). The pattern is the Passover's: the indignation falls, and God's people are behind a door while it passes. That is where the whole idea of refuge lives: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overpass as to pass over; to cross; to overlook; and overpast as passed by, gone by, or ended.
webster_full: OVERP'ASS, v.t. To pass over; to cross; as, to overpass a stream.
1. To overlook; to pass with disregard.
2. Not to receive; to omit.
OVERP'AST, pp. Passed by; gone by; ended.
Until these calamities be overpast. Ps. 57. Hide thyself until the indignation be overpast. Is. 26.
scriptures: Psalm 57:1

To the chief Musician, Altaschith, Michtam of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave. Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast.
Isaiah 26:20
Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast.
Isaiah 26:21
For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity: the earth also shall disclose her blood, and shall no more cover her slain.
Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
corruption_summary: The promise of shelter is either inflated into a guarantee of exemption from suffering or dissolved into a figure of speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 91 has been printed on a great many cards and preached as a guarantee that no harm will come near a believer, which the martyrs disprove and which Satan himself quoted in the wilderness. What Psalm 57:1 actually shows is the shape of the promise: David is in a cave, hunted by a king, and what he claims is the shadow of wings until these calamities be overpast. The shelter is real and it is not an exemption. He is covered in the trouble, not lifted out of it, and the trouble has an end appointed by Someone else.

Isaiah 26:20 is the text some have pressed into service for a pre-tribulation removal of the church, and it will not bear the weight — the chambers are on the earth, the doors are shut from the inside, and the people wait out a little moment while the LORD comes out of His place. The dictionary's reading is the plain one and the older one: this is Passover, and Noah's ark, and the cave at Adullam. God's people are kept through the indignation behind a door He appointed. The comfort is not that the storm will miss them but that it has a term, and that the One who sets the term is the One who told them where to stand.
roots_summary: Hebrew abar (H5674), to pass over, pass by; za'am (H2195), indignation; chasah (H2620), to take refuge.
roots_lines: Hebrew ya'abor (H5674) — shall pass over; the verb behind overpast, and the same root as the Passover's passing over.
Hebrew za'am (H2195) — indignation, fury; Isaiah 26:20, a wrath with a stated duration.
Hebrew echseh (H2620) — I will take refuge; Psalm 57:1, in the shadow of the wings.
Hebrew kim'at rega — as it were for a little moment; Isaiah 26:20, the term of the hiding.
Hebrew sether elyon (H5643) — the secret place of the most High; Psalm 91:1, the same shelter named.
usage: “Until these calamities be overpast” — written in a cave, with a king hunting him.
“Shut thy doors about thee” — the doors are shut from the inside.
“For a little moment” — the comfort is the term, not the absence of the storm.

pos: pp. (held up; sustained; supported — the older participle of uphold)
etymology: From up and hold, with the strong participial ending the Authorized Version preserves; modern English says upheld. The picture is a hand placed underneath something that would otherwise go down.
biblical_def: Two occurrences, and they answer a question worth asking: what holds a man up, and what holds a throne up? Of a man, and the agency is words: “Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees” (Job 4:4). This is Eliphaz reminding Job of his own former ministry, and the irony is thick — the counsel Job once gave others is about to fail him from the mouths of his friends. But the observation itself is true and the Bible endorses it elsewhere: speech holds people up. A man falling has been caught by a sentence more than once. Of a throne: “Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy” (Pro 20:28). Not by force, not by revenue, not by fear — by mercy and truth together, which is the pairing Scripture uses of God's own character. Behind both stands the hand that does the actual holding: “I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isa 41:10); and “Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand” (Psa 37:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uphold as to lift on high; to elevate; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling or declining; and to keep from being lost.
webster_full: UPHO'LD, v.t. [up and hold.] pret. and pp. upheld. Upholden is obsolete.
1. To lift on high; to elevate.
2. To support; to sustain; to keep erect; to keep from falling.
Thy words have upholden him that was falling. Job 4.
3. To keep from declining; to support in any state. His throne is upholden by mercy. Prov. 20. 4. To continue without failing.
scriptures: Job 4:4
Thy words have upholden him that was falling, and thou hast strengthened the feeble knees.
Proverbs 20:28
Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.
Isaiah 41:10
Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Psalm 37:24
Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
corruption_summary: Power is assumed to be upheld by strength, and speech is assumed to be weightless — and Scripture reverses both.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 20:28 is a startling piece of political theology: a throne is upheld by mercy. Every instinct of statecraft says otherwise — a ruler is secured by power, wealth, surveillance, or the fear he can generate. Solomon, who had all four, says the thing that actually holds a throne up is mercy and truth, the same pair used of the LORD Himself in Exodus 34:6. That is not a sentimental claim. A ruler who is neither merciful nor truthful must hold his place by force alone, and force is expensive and eventually insufficient. The Christian magistrate is a minister of God for good, and the qualities that keep him in place are the qualities of the God he serves.

Job 4:4 cuts the other way against a culture that treats words as weightless while also treating them as weapons. Eliphaz's observation is accurate: Job's words had held up men who were falling and strengthened feeble knees. What follows in the book is the demonstration that words can also crush, because Eliphaz and his friends proceed to spend thirty chapters doing exactly that to a man already on the ground. The same instrument that catches a falling man can finish him. That is why James puts the tongue at the centre of practical religion, and why the church's ordinary ministry of encouragement is not a minor thing — it is a hand under an elbow, and the hand under all of it is God's own (Isa 41:10).
roots_summary: Hebrew qum (H6965), to raise up, establish; sa'ad (H5582), to support, sustain; tamak (H8551), to grasp, uphold.
roots_lines: Hebrew yeqimun (H6965) — they raised up, set on his feet; Job 4:4, of words holding a falling man.
Hebrew sa'ad (H5582) — to support, uphold, sustain; Proverbs 20:28, of the throne held by mercy.
Hebrew chesed we'emeth (H2617, H571) — mercy and truth; the pair of Exodus 34:6, here holding up a king.
Hebrew tamakti (H8551) — I have grasped, upheld; Isaiah 41:10, the right hand of His righteousness.
Hebrew somekh (H5564) — upholding, leaning upon; Psalm 37:24, the LORD's hand under the falling man.
usage: “Thy words have upholden him that was falling” — and the same friends then crushed him.
“His throne is upholden by mercy” — not by force, which runs out.
“Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down” — the hand is underneath.
